decisions.reason: SOL keeps the image and uses a brisker sentence break.
SOL preserves the formation and the man at its head; the opening “And” reflects the Korean transition.
“Returned his smile” naturally conveys the narrator responding with a faint smile.
SOL keeps the offer to spend time on the meeting and the need to speak in person without the stiff repetition of “precious.”
“Sound as if” keeps the Emperor’s observation and reads naturally.
SOL keeps the admission that he did not expect the Emperor to be waiting and the pleasure at seeing him.
SOL preserves the contrast between being glad to see the Emperor and being glad to see the others.
SOL uses the established Imperial Capital and North Gate terms in a natural possessive construction.
The Korean points at something with “That…”; SOL’s “Oh” changes the reaction and drops the pointing cue.
The Korean says Hogun was the first and most frequently seen face at the imperial court; SOL’s “first of them I’d met” changes that context.
SOL keeps the same people and timing; the tighter phrasing does not change the sense.
“Imperial Younger Brother” follows the binding glossary for 황태제.
“With his only family” preserves the boy being together with family.
“Sat in his saddle” preserves the horseback image and reads naturally.
The punctuation change does not alter the meaning or voice.
The Korean describes a suppressed, restrained voice; “low” changes that vocal quality.
SOL preserves the brief glare and the Emperor’s release of the laughter he had held back.
The Emperor’s amazement and the charge of arrogance and rudeness remain intact.
“Just a rogue” keeps the self-description without BASE’s redundant “nothing more than a mere.”
SOL preserves the gasps; the preceding reply already makes their cause clear.
SOL says the ministers had been brought there, adding an agent and changing the source’s uncertainty about why they were there.
“I see” keeps the Emperor’s realization.
The pronoun has a clear referent, so omitting “the Emperor” changes no meaning.
The Korean says he merits everyone’s admiration; SOL weakens that to respect.
It preserves the clip-clop sound and italicizes the sound effect consistently with the prose.
The Korean explicitly says he suddenly brought his hand to his shoulder; SOL drops the sudden movement.
“Without hesitation” keeps the action and the Emperor’s faint smile.
SOL preserves the ministers’ shock and the dragon cloak image in tighter prose.
The Korean says the voices were swallowed by the wind along with the Emperor’s command; SOL drops the wind image.
SOL drops the heavy silence’s effect on those around them and the Emperor’s act of turning his gaze to the narrator.
“Go on” naturally urges him to accept the gift.
“No ordinary gift” preserves the narrator’s recognition of its significance.
The narrator’s objection that the gift is far from small remains clear.
SOL keeps both reasons the cloak is extraordinary, with the dragon’s importance foregrounded.
“A single dragon” preserves the one-dragon image.
The emblem’s meaning is unchanged in the more compact phrasing.
“Answered in disbelief” naturally conveys his incredulous response.
SOL preserves his hesitation at the sudden turn and the Emperor’s firmness.
The Korean says something regrettable will happen; SOL changes that certainty to “might.”
SOL keeps the narrator’s skepticism about being reassured in natural dialogue.
“It’s just you” preserves the Emperor’s teasing dismissal of the narrator’s reaction.
The contrastive phrasing preserves that they had known each other only briefly but already understood one another.
The complete thought reads naturally while preserving the realization that they were alike.
SOL makes the general “made sacrifices” more specific by saying he sacrificed himself.
The omitted “choice” is clear from context and the lack of regret remains intact.
The Korean calls the Emperor just one human being; SOL drops that emphasis with “was human.”
The recast keeps the image of one person doing his best from where he stood.
The article change leaves the cloak and the Emperor’s satisfied look unchanged.
“The next words made me doubt my ears” preserves the reaction to what the Emperor says.
“Name … Marquis” naturally conveys the Emperor conferring the title.
The voice breaking the deep-night silence preserves the force of the declaration.
SOL keeps the declaration ringing out and the commoners gathering around the guards’ torches.
The Emperor’s continuing solemn declaration is preserved in a natural lead-in.
SOL keeps the fief, listed Shanxi locations, and household revenues; the recast remains source-faithful.
The Korean emphasizes that the flash suddenly leapt from his waist; SOL drops that suddenness.
“Grant you the post” accurately conveys conferring the Thousand Captain position and issuing the command.
“My chest thudded” preserves the bodily pounding described in the Korean.
“That wasn’t my heartbeat” keeps the correction and reads naturally.
The Korean says the guards stamped their feet forcefully; SOL drops the intensity.
“Merely as an escort” preserves the point that escort duty was not their only purpose.
“Force” preserves the punitive military body without overstating its scale as an army.
The added “he’d” resolves the prepared reinforcements to the Emperor without changing the sense.
The ringing-ear sensation is retained in the following hunk, so this standalone repetition can be removed.
SOL combines the ringing ears, bells, and surrounding cheers without dropping any of those sensations.
“Two” preserves the number of revolution plotters, clear from context.
The Korean specifies rewards for those departing; SOL preserves that detail and the uprooting of the traitors.
“Every deed has its due” naturally preserves the idea that actions bring fitting recompense.
The answer follows immediately in dialogue, so omitting “answered” loses no information.
The fading spark and warmth through the Emperor’s fingertips remain intact.
The flowing voice and quiet addition are preserved in a natural construction.
“Someone who shines a light upon this world” naturally conveys a person who brightens the world.
The Korean compares the words to a final will or testament; “final farewell” replaces that image.
The Korean describes the moment of parting as bitter and full of regret; SOL’s “something to be wished for” shifts the sense.
The source says moisture fell onto the saddle; SOL specifies tears, which the line itself does not.
SOL drops that the Emperor spoke calmly, an explicit characterization in the source.
The shorter question keeps the Emperor’s inquiry about the boy’s sadness.
“Imperial Younger Brother” follows the binding glossary for 황태제.
The Korean’s “희한하구나” is emphatic; BASE’s “very strange” preserves that force.
“Sorry to see them go” naturally conveys the Emperor’s regret at their departure and contrasts with the boy’s claimed lack of sadness.
The Korean says the Emperor’s smiling face was reflected in Zhu Bao’s eyes; SOL changes that image to his face filling them.
“Too stunned to answer” preserves the boy’s blank, unresponsive state before the Emperor speaks gently.
“Needn’t start swallowing your feelings” keeps the advice not to force himself to suppress them.
The proverb and its warning that accumulated endurance turns poisonous are preserved.
The stammer in “H-hyung” preserves the source’s broken attempt to address his brother.
SOL omits the Emperor riding away, an explicit action in the source.
“Repeated something someone had once told him” naturally introduces the remembered words.
The line keeps the shared humanity and the sense of “in the end” without BASE’s added “only.”
The following sentence incorporates the sobs and the Emperor’s thought, so the separate setup can be removed.
The hope that Zhu Bao will not follow the Emperor’s path is preserved; “at least” reflects the source’s emphasis on him.
The Korean leaves what he realized unstated; SOL adds “it” to the thought.
The gate closing and the horse galloping through it remain clear, with the source’s sequence intact.
The Korean explicitly identifies the returning figure as “that man”; SOL’s “That’s…” drops the reference.
SOL omits the Emperor’s confusion and the fact that he asked the returning man a question.
The Korean says the Divine Physician smiled and continued speaking; SOL drops the continuation cue.
